abstract: Neural information processing is inextricably linked to the selectivity of individual neurons, as described by their receptive fields. Far from the sensory periphery, neural representations are the result of substantial upstream processing, mixed with internally generated information. Low-dimensional spatial codes in the hippocampal formation offer a handle on understanding these representations. The subiculum, a key but comparatively understudied hippocampal area, exhibits numerous, seemingly unrelated neural codes. Neurons like boundary vector cells, corner cells, or axis-tuned cells are named after the environmental features that appear to drive them, but a common account for their neuronal selectivity is lacking. Here, we propose Disco, a theory explaining subicular functions and related neural codes in other areas. Given the continuous flow of experience, subicular activity can be understood as signaling discontinuities in that flow, coded in a vector base. Geometric discontinuities drive responses to walls, drops, objects, holes, corners, and curved surfaces. The generality of Disco enables predictions for 3D environments, natural scenes, and mixed-modality coding. Discontinuities are not identical to the concept of boundaries (abstract or spatial), as illustrated by non-spatial discontinuities in behavioral state. These yield axis coding in the model (activity along parallel maze arms). Finally, tracking population activity signals event boundaries as discontinuities in neural space. The emergence of diverse neural activity suggests that discontinuity coding may serve as a key principle in the subiculum and related brain areas supporting (spatial) memory and navigation.
